readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 18:1-23:18. This is another survey day. The oracles continue against Cush, Egypt, Babylon, Edom, Arabia, Jerusalem, and Tyre. Look for the repeated message: do not put your trust in the nations.
settingTheScene: The oracles against the nations continue. Judah was tempted to look to Egypt and Cush (Ethiopia) for protection against Assyria, and Isaiah repeatedly warns against it. One of the strangest passages in the book appears in chapter 20, where Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years as a sign of what would happen to Egypt and Cush. Chapter 22 turns the oracles back toward Jerusalem itself.
observation: “In that time a present will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth-skinned” (18:7).
“The LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas” (19:22).
“Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance” (19:25).
“Thus shall it be with the nations in which we hoped… and how shall we escape?” (20:6).
“You were not looking to him who did it, or have regard for him who planned it long ago” (22:11).
“And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David” (22:22).
“Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD” (23:18).
interpretation:
The oracles of these chapters appear dry, but they carry a thread of astonishing hope. Egypt, the old oppressor of Israel, will be struck by the LORD and then healed. In chapter 19, there is a vision of a day when Egypt will speak the language of Canaan, build an altar to the LORD, and cry out to him. He will send them a savior, and they will know him. And then the climax: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.” Three nations, former enemies, become a blessing in the midst of the earth. The gospel of God’s mercy for the nations is already in the Old Testament.

The oracle of chapter 20 is bizarre but purposeful. Isaiah’s three years of walking naked and barefoot is a sermon without words: this is how the Egyptians and Ethiopians will be led away by Assyria. Those who relied on them will say, “Where can we escape?” It was designed to make Judah afraid of putting hope in the wrong place.

Chapter 22 is the oracle about Jerusalem, “the valley of vision.” The city celebrates when it should mourn. People prepare their defenses, store water, fortify the walls, and count houses, but “you did not look to him who did it.” They prepared everything but did not seek God. The result is a dreadful motto: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 15:32. The chapter also contains the story of Shebna, a proud steward replaced by Eliakim, who receives “the key of the house of David.” He can open, and none can shut.

The last oracle, against Tyre, ends with a surprise: her profits will be set apart for the LORD. The nations are not simply doomed. Some are redeemed.
connection: Revelation 3:7 speaks of Christ as the one “who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut.” Acts 8:26-40 records an Ethiopian official coming to faith. Ephesians 2:13-14 says that those who were far off have been brought near. Galatians 3:8 says the gospel was preached beforehand to Abraham: “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” Revelation 21:24 pictures the nations bringing their glory into the city.
application:
Where are you trusting in something other than God for security: a job, savings, relationships, a plan?

Pray for a nation or group you would not usually pray for, including those who have been enemies.

Remember that the keys of the kingdom are in the hands of Jesus, and bring a closed door to him in prayer.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you look to Egypt, to people or things, for help.
Pray for the nations to be brought into his kingdom.
Thank him that his plan stands.
